hook: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. The skeleton of every written answer and a good habit for MBE reasoning: name the issue, state the rule, apply it to THESE facts, then pick the answer. On the MBE the fight is almost always in the A.
subject: General

hook: Conclusion, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion: state your answer first and last so the reader (or grader) never has to hunt for it. Same family as IRAC, TREAT, CRAAC.
subject: General

hook: The MBE asks for the BEST answer, not a true statement. Two options can both be legally true; the winner is the one that answers THIS question with THIS rule. Read the call of the question first, then the facts.
subject: General
note: Study-skill framing, not a rule of law; NCBE page only confirms format (200 questions, 175 scored + 25 pretest, two 3-hour sessions).

hook: Marriage (promise made IN CONSIDERATION of marriage, e.g. a prenup, not mutual promises to marry), Year (cannot be performed within one year of MAKING the contract), Land (any interest in real property), Executor (executor/administrator promises to pay estate debts from OWN funds), Goods ($500 or more, UCC 2-201), Surety (promise to answer for another's debt). All six need a signed writing.
subject: Contracts
note: The MY LEGS letters are verified against UCC 2-201 and secondary outlines. 'Year' test is whether performance is POSSIBLE inside a year, not likely; clock starts at formation. Surety has the 'main purpose' (own economic benefit) exception. Restatement (Second) of Contracts 110 lists the non-goods five.

hook: Ask 'could this possibly be finished in 364 days?' If yes, no writing needed, even if everyone knows it will take longer. A contract 'for life' is outside the statute because the promisor could die within a year.
subject: Contracts
note: Lifetime contracts: majority view per the cited outline; check the call of the question.

hook: Specially manufactured goods, Admission in court, Merchant's confirmation, Payment/acceptance. Four ways a $500+ goods deal survives without the buyer's/seller's own signed writing. Remember: payment/acceptance saves only the goods paid for or accepted, and an admission only the quantity admitted.
subject: Contracts
note: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text). (A popular 'SWAMP' mnemonic adds 'Waiver', which is NOT a 2-201 exception, so we avoid it.)

hook: Merchants: if you get a written confirmation and say nothing in writing within 10 days of receipt, you can no longer raise the statute of frauds against it. It does NOT prove the quantity or that a deal existed; it only removes the defense.
subject: Contracts

hook: Firm offer (UCC 2-205: merchant, signed writing, up to 3 months), Option contract (paid for), Unilateral offer once performance has begun, Reasonable foreseeable Reliance. Four exceptions to 'an offer can be revoked any time before acceptance'.
subject: Contracts
note: FOUR is the JD Advising mnemonic; mapped to UCC 2-205 (fetched) and Restatement (Second) 25, 45, 87(2) (from memory).

hook: Death/incapacity of offeror, Rejection, Counteroffer, Lapse of time, Revocation. Five ways an offer ends before it is accepted. A counteroffer is a rejection plus a new offer, so 'I accept but only if you add X' ends the original (common law mirror image rule).
source: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text)
subject: Contracts
note: Our own mnemonic; the five terminators are standard black-letter law (Restatement (Second) 36).

hook: Between merchants, an extra term in the acceptance becomes part of the deal under 2-207(2) UNLESS: Offer limits acceptance to its terms, the term Materially alters the deal, or Notice of objection was already given/given in reasonable time. O-M-N = the three escapes. Common law instead uses the mirror image rule.
subject: Contracts

hook: If the paperwork never matches but both sides ship and accept the goods, there is still a contract. Its terms are the terms the writings AGREE on, plus UCC gap-fillers. This is the 'knockout' result.
subject: Contracts

hook: Changing the duty on one side, Lawsuit settlement of a good-faith claim, Unforeseen difficulties, Sale of goods (UCC 2-209 needs no consideration for a modification), Time-barred debt (new promise), Extra person, Release. Moments when a promise to do what you already must do still counts.
subject: Contracts
note: From JD Advising; individual items match Restatement (Second) 73, 74, 89, 82 and UCC 2-209 from memory, not re-fetched.

topic: Perfect tender vs. cure vs. revocation
hook: UCC buyer ladder: reject for ANY nonconformity (perfect tender, 2-601) within a reasonable time; seller may cure (2-508); if you ACCEPTED, you may revoke only for substantial impairment, with notice, within a reasonable time (2-608).
subject: Contracts
note: 2-608 fetched; 2-601 and 2-508 cited from memory.

hook: Implied warranty of merchantability (UCC 2-314) arises only when the seller is a MERCHANT in goods of that kind. Minimum: passes in the trade, fair average quality, fit for ordinary purposes, even kind/quality, adequately packaged/labeled, matches label promises. 'Ordinary use', not 'perfect'.
subject: Contracts

hook: Courts look at the unfair PROCESS (no real choice, fine print, pressure) and unfair TERMS (one-sided). Tested as of the time the contract was MADE, and the court may refuse, cut the clause, or limit it (UCC 2-302).
subject: Contracts

topic: Damages must be Foreseeable, Certain, Unavoidable
hook: Contract damages checklist: foreseeable at formation (Hadley), proven with reasonable certainty, and not avoidable by reasonable mitigation. Three filters between a breach and a check.
subject: Contracts
note: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text); maps to Restatement (Second) 351, 352, 350.

hook: Motive, Intent, Mistake (absence of), Identity, Common plan. Non-propensity reasons to admit a prior bad act. Caution: the rule's real list is longer (motive, opportunity, intent, preparation, plan, knowledge, identity, absence of mistake, lack of accident) and is illustrative ('such as'). Never 'he did it before, so he did it again'.
subject: Evidence
note: MIMIC covers only part of the rule text; treat it as a prompt, not a closed list.

hook: In a criminal case the prosecution can't start the character fight; the DEFENDANT does (his own trait, or the victim's). Then the prosecution may rebut and, if the victim's trait was attacked, offer the defendant's same trait. In homicide, evidence the victim was the first aggressor opens the door to the victim's peacefulness.
subject: Evidence

hook: Stating a privilege (court rules it applies), Absent (proponent can't get attendance or testimony by process or reasonable means), Ill or dead (infirmity), Lacks memory, Stubborn refusal (despite a court order). Five roads to 'unavailable', which unlocks every 804(b) exception.
subject: Evidence
note: SAILS verified item by item against 804(a)(1)-(5). Note the proponent cannot have procured the unavailability.

hook: Former testimony, Against interest, Dying declaration, Family history, Forfeiture by wrongdoing. Five exceptions that need an unavailable declarant. Dying declarations only in homicide prosecutions and civil cases, not every criminal case.
subject: Evidence
note: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text). (804(b)(5) is transferred to Rule 807, the residual exception.)

topic: Timeline of the first four 803 exceptions
hook: Present sense impression = live commentary ('he's running the light!'); excited utterance = still shaking from the event; then-existing condition = how I feel or what I plan NOW; medical = said to a provider to get diagnosed/treated. Availability of the declarant is irrelevant for all 23 exceptions in 803.
subject: Evidence
note: Condition statements about memory or belief ('I think he hit me') are excluded, except for the validity or terms of the declarant's will.

topic: A through E of 801(d)(2) (opposing party's statements)
hook: (A) Alone: the party's own words; (B) Believed/adopted; (C) Commissioned speaker; (D) Dependent: agent or employee on a matter within the scope; (E) Everyone in the conspiracy, during and in furtherance. Not hearsay when offered AGAINST that party. The letters follow the rule's own letters.
subject: Evidence
note: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text)

hook: Verbal acts (legally operative words, e.g. a contract offer), Impeachment (prior inconsistent statement used only for credibility), Circumstantial state of mind of the declarant, Effect on the listener (notice, motive, reasonableness). If the statement is not offered to prove the TRUTH of what it asserts, it is not hearsay (801(c)).
subject: Evidence
note: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text). The four categories are standard doctrine; 801(c) definition fetched.

topic: 609: felons get balanced, liars get in
hook: Impeaching by conviction: a crime punishable by more than a year gets Rule 403-style balancing (stricter for a criminal defendant); a crime of dishonest act or false statement (crimen falsi) comes in automatically. Ten-year limit runs from conviction or release, whichever is later.
subject: Evidence

topic: Voir dire the expert: 702 'more likely than not'
hook: Since Dec 2023, the proponent must show the court it is MORE LIKELY THAN NOT that the expert's knowledge helps the jury, rests on sufficient facts/data, uses reliable methods, and applies them reliably. 'Knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education': experience alone can qualify.
subject: Evidence

hook: A juror may NOT testify about deliberations, a juror's mental process, or how something affected a vote. Three doors stay open: extraneous prejudicial information, outside influence, and a clerical mistake on the verdict form.
subject: Evidence

hook: Defenses 12(b)(2) personal jurisdiction, (3) venue, (4) process, (5) service are WAIVED if you omit them from your first Rule 12 motion or from your answer. Subject-matter jurisdiction (b)(1) is never waived (12(h)(3)); failure to state a claim and Rule 19 joinder survive to trial (12(h)(2)).
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: Commonality, Adequacy, Numerosity, Typicality are the four 23(a) prerequisites. The 'S' (Superiority) belongs only to Rule 23(b)(3) money-damages classes (with Predominance), not to every class. Then pick a 23(b) type: (1) inconsistent adjudications, (2) injunction/declaratory relief, (3) predominance + superiority.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: Ten depositions per side, one day of seven hours each, 25 interrogatories (including discrete subparts). Everything beyond needs a stipulation or court leave.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: A sanctions motion must first be SERVED, and cannot be filed until 21 days pass without the challenged paper being withdrawn or corrected. The certification covers purpose, law, facts, and denials after reasonable inquiry.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: Harm irreparable without it, Equities balance, Likelihood of success, Public interest. The four Winter v. NRDC factors. (A TRO runs on the same factors but is short-lived.)
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Mapping matches Winter v. NRDC (2008) from memory; the JD Advising list was the fetched source.

hook: 28 U.S.C. 1332: no plaintiff may share a state of citizenship with any defendant (Strawbridge v. Curtiss) AND the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. An individual is a citizen of her DOMICILE; a corporation of its state of incorporation and its nerve center (Hertz).
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Hertz fetched; 1332 and Strawbridge cited from memory.

hook: Continuous, Hostile (without the owner's permission), Actual possession, Notorious (open and visible), Goes on for the statutory period, Exclusive. Meet all six for the whole period and title shifts to the possessor.
subject: Real Property
note: CHANGE mapping verified against the JD Advising list; 'Heluva' (Hostile, Exclusive, Lasting, Uninterrupted, Visible, Actual) is the same elements. Majority view: hostile means 'without permission', no bad faith needed.

hook: Time, Title, Interest, Possession: the four unities a joint tenancy needs at creation (same time, same instrument, equal shares, equal right to possess the whole). Lose a unity and it becomes a tenancy in common. Tenancy by the entirety adds marriage.
subject: Real Property

hook: Give it away (conveyance), Sign a contract for sale (see note), Actual foreclosure or judicial sale, Mortgage in a title-theory state. NOT severing: a will (survivorship wins), or a joint tenant's death.
subject: Real Property
note: Treat the 'S' with caution: whether an executory contract to sell severs varies (equitable conversion). Check the call of the question.

topic: PINT and TIN (covenants running with land)
hook: Real covenant at law: Privity (horizontal and vertical), Intent, Notice, Touch and concern. Equitable servitude: Touch and concern, Intent, Notice (no privity). A writing is also required for both (except implied reciprocal servitudes). Tulk v. Moxhay is the origin of the equitable version.
subject: Real Property

hook: Prescription, Express grant/reservation, Necessity, Implication (prior use), Estoppel. Five ways to create an easement. Express needs a writing (statute of frauds); necessity ends when the necessity ends; prescription copies adverse possession.
source: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text)
subject: Real Property
note: Our own mnemonic; creation methods match Restatement (Third) of Property (Servitudes) 2.1-2.16 from memory.

hook: Race: first to record wins. Notice: a later bona fide purchaser WITHOUT notice beats an earlier unrecorded deed. Race-notice: a BFP without notice wins only if she also records first. Notice (actual, record, inquiry) is judged when she buys.
subject: Real Property
note: Standard doctrine; page not re-fetched in this session.

hook: 'No interest is good unless it must vest, if at all, not later than 21 years after some life in being at the creation of the interest.' (Gray). Test it at creation, by what MIGHT happen. Typical killers: the fertile octogenarian, the unborn widow, the slothful executor.
subject: Real Property
note: Check the question for wait-and-see, USRAP (90 years) or abolition; the MBE outline lists future interests and RAP.

topic: Determinable vs. condition subsequent: the magic words
hook: 'So long as / while / until' = fee simple determinable: ends AUTOMATICALLY, possibility of reverter. 'But if / provided that / on condition that' = fee simple subject to condition subsequent: needs the grantor to ACT (right of entry).
subject: Real Property

topic: Equitable conversion: risk passes at signing
hook: Once a land contract is signed, the buyer is the equitable owner and (majority rule) bears the risk of loss unless the seller is at fault or the contract says otherwise. Insure at signing, not at closing.
subject: Real Property
note: Some states follow the Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act instead.

hook: Channels, Instrumentalities, Substantial effects. Lopez (1995) names the three categories of Congress's commerce power. Prong three needs ECONOMIC activity in the aggregate (Wickard yes; gun possession near a school, Lopez no).
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: Race, National origin, Alienage (state laws; federal alienage classifications get rational basis). Strict scrutiny: necessary to a compelling interest, narrowly tailored, burden on the government. Intermediate: gender and non-marital status (substantially related to an important interest).
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Classification list from standard doctrine; alienage nuance (Graham v. Richardson vs Mathews v. Diaz) from memory.

hook: Injury in fact (concrete, particularized, actual or imminent), Causation (traceable to the defendant), Redressability (a win likely helps). Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992). Plus ripeness and mootness: the case must be live.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: Serious Literary, Artistic, Political, or Scientific value. Material is obscene only if (1) the average person, by contemporary community standards, finds it appeals to the prurient interest, (2) it depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way defined by state law, and (3) lacks SLAPS value.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: SLAPS is a widely used mnemonic; the three prongs verified against Miller summary.

hook: Content-neutral rules survive if narrowly tailored to a significant government interest AND they leave open ample alternative channels. Content-BASED rules get strict scrutiny. Ask first: is the rule about the message?
subject: Constitutional Law
note: From memory (Ward v. Rock Against Racism); not re-fetched.

topic: Lemon is out, history is in
hook: Lemon's three prongs (secular purpose, primary effect, no entanglement) are no longer the governing test: Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022) looks to 'historical practices and understandings'. If an old answer key says 'apply Lemon', check its date.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Court said it relied on history in place of Lemon and the endorsement test; a later decision (Groff v. DeJoy) called Lemon abrogated.

hook: Marriage (Obergefell), Obscenity at home (Stanley), Parental rights, Procreation/contraception (Griswold), Sexual intimacy (Lawrence). Abortion is NOT on the fundamental-rights list after Dobbs (2022): rational basis, with the Glucksberg 'deeply rooted in history and tradition' test for new rights.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Mnemonic from JD Advising; Dobbs caveat is our addition.

hook: A popular mnemonic lists political-question topics, but one item (qualifications of Congress) is wrong as a blanket rule: Powell v. McCormack held Congress cannot exclude a duly elected member who meets the constitutional qualifications. Learn the Baker v. Carr markers instead (textual commitment, no manageable standards).
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Marked uncertain: do not ship SCREAM as written. Powell v. McCormack and Nixon v. United States cited from memory.

hook: Exigent circumstances, Search incident to arrest, Consent, Automobile, Plain view, Inventory, Special needs, Terry stop-and-frisk. Updated rule: a car search incident to arrest requires the arrestee within reaching distance or reason to believe evidence of the crime of arrest is inside (Arizona v. Gant, 2009). Old guides that let police search the whole passenger compartment are out of date.
subject: Criminal Procedure
note: ESCAPIST letters verified; the source's auto-search sentence is pre-Gant. Gant cited from memory.

topic: IIA + G (what cleans a tainted fruit)
hook: Independent source, Inevitable discovery, Attenuation: the three taint-removers after an illegal search. Add the Good-faith exception (Leon) and you have the four big limits on the exclusionary rule that appear on the exam.
subject: Criminal Procedure
note: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text); Mapp fetched, Wong Sun/Nix/Strieff/Leon cited from memory.

topic: SICK (when the exclusionary rule doesn't apply)
hook: Standing (you can't assert someone else's rights), Impeachment (illegally obtained evidence can still impeach the defendant), Civil and other proceedings (grand jury, civil, parole), Knock-and-announce violations (Hudson). Companion to IIA + G.
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: No warnings needed unless the person is in CUSTODY and being INTERROGATED by the state, and the statement is offered against them. Noncustodial silence is not protected unless you expressly invoke (Salinas v. Texas); ambiguous requests don't stop questioning (Berghuis v. Thompkins).
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: Fifth (Miranda/Edwards): attaches in custodial interrogation, applies to any crime. Sixth: attaches at formal charge, and is OFFENSE-SPECIFIC (Texas v. Cobb). Once a suspect invokes the Fifth Amendment right to counsel, police must stop (Edwards) unless the suspect restarts the talk; the Sixth Amendment right covers critical stages of the charged offense only.
subject: Criminal Procedure

topic: Possession vs. title: four property crimes
hook: Larceny = take possession without consent, intending to permanently deprive. Larceny by trick = they give you POSSESSION because you lied. False pretenses = they give you TITLE because you lied. Embezzlement = you ALREADY lawfully hold it and convert it.
subject: Criminal Law
note: Standard common-law distinctions; page not re-fetched.

hook: Purposely, Knowingly, Recklessly, Negligently: from most to least culpable. Each higher state satisfies the lower ones. Recklessness = consciously disregarding a substantial and unjustifiable risk; negligence = should have been aware.
subject: Criminal Law
note: MPC 2.02 from memory; Wex mens rea page not re-fetched.

hook: Intent to Kill, intent to cause Grievous bodily harm, Depraved-heart (extreme indifference), Felony murder. The mental state called 'malice aforethought' can be satisfied four ways. Provocation (heat of passion) mitigates to voluntary manslaughter.
subject: Criminal Law

hook: Burglary, Arson, Rape, Robbery, Kidnapping: the classic common-law felony-murder felonies (the MPC lists robbery, rape, arson, burglary, kidnapping, felonious escape as a presumption of extreme indifference). Usually the question gives the statute; remember merger (assault can't be the predicate) and 'inherently dangerous'.
subject: Criminal Law
note: BARRK is a secondary-source mnemonic. Wikipedia lists the MPC's felonies, not the common-law list. Verify against a primary source before shipping.

hook: Attempt and solicitation MERGE into the completed crime (you can't be convicted of both). Conspiracy does NOT merge, and each co-conspirator is liable for reasonably foreseeable crimes of the others in furtherance (Pinkerton).
subject: Criminal Law

hook: 'You shall have the body': the opening command of the writ that orders a jailer to bring the prisoner before a judge. You already say it; on the exam it is the way a detainee (including a state prisoner in federal court) challenges the lawfulness of confinement. The Suspension Clause (Art. I, 9) protects it.
subject: Evidence

hook: 'The thing speaks for itself.' When an accident of this kind doesn't normally happen without negligence, the jury may infer breach. Born in Byrne v. Boadle (1863): a barrel of flour falls from a warehouse window onto a passer-by. Elements: ordinarily doesn't happen without negligence; instrumentality in the defendant's control; not caused by the plaintiff.
subject: Torts
note: Elements from Restatement (Second) of Torts 328D, from memory.

hook: 'Guilty mind': the mental element of a crime (purpose, knowledge, recklessness, negligence). From the maxim 'actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea'. Strict-liability offences need none.
subject: Criminal Law

hook: 'Guilty act': the voluntary physical act (or an omission where there is a legal duty). Mens rea + actus reus must concur in time. The famous pair: you need both to convict.
subject: Criminal Law

hook: 'To stand by things decided': courts follow their own precedent and higher courts' precedent. Horizontal (own court) is flexible; vertical (higher court) is binding. Re-read the question: 'binding authority' vs 'persuasive authority'.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: Not Latin at all: Anglo-Norman law French, 'to speak the truth' (a juror's or witness's oath). In the US it means (1) questioning prospective jurors and (2) questioning a witness or expert on competence/qualifications before testimony. Bar-exam relevance: voir dire of an expert under FRE 702.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Same 'true' root as 'verdict' (veir 'true' + dit 'said'): verdict = true saying.

hook: 'To be informed': a writ by which a higher court asks the lower court to send up the record. At the Supreme Court it means discretionary review: the Court grants 'cert' in a small fraction of petitions. It is not an appeal of right.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: 'We command': an order compelling an official to perform a clear, non-discretionary duty. Marbury v. Madison asked for it against the Secretary of State and lost on jurisdiction.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: 'At first face': enough evidence to win unless rebutted. A prima facie case shifts the burden of production to the other side. Also the standard in Rule 12/56 thinking: has the plaintiff shown enough for a jury?
subject: Evidence

hook: 'In the place of a parent': a school or custodian standing in for the parent. Think of Tinker-style school-speech questions and the duty to supervise.
subject: Torts
note: Constitutional school-speech link is our gloss; the Latin meaning is verified.

hook: 'For oneself': representing yourself without a lawyer. A criminal defendant has a Sixth Amendment right to self-representation (Faretta) if the waiver is knowing and voluntary.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Faretta from memory.

hook: 'For the good' (pro bono publico, for the public good): work done without fee. Some jurisdictions now require pro bono hours for admission; the Latin is the first thing a 1L learns.
subject: General

hook: 'This for that': the bargained-for exchange. Consideration in one phrase: each side's promise or performance is the price of the other. Gifts and past consideration fail it.
subject: Contracts

hook: 'From a thing done afterward': a law that punishes conduct that was legal when done, or increases the punishment. Banned for Congress (Art. I, 9, cl. 3) and the states (Art. I, 10). Applies to criminal punishments, not civil regulations.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: 'At the threshold': a pretrial motion asking the judge to rule on admissibility before the jury hears anything ('motion in limine'). A definitive ruling preserves the objection (FRE 103).
subject: Evidence
note: FRE 103 preservation point from memory.

hook: 'In the chamber': the judge reviews something privately, outside open court. Typical use: reviewing privileged documents to decide privilege or relevance.
subject: Evidence

hook: 'From one party': an application heard with only one side present. TROs can sometimes issue ex parte, but only with a strong showing of immediate irreparable harm and notice efforts (Rule 65(b)).
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Rule 65(b) from memory.

hook: 'Of its own accord': the court acts without a motion. Subject-matter jurisdiction is the classic example: the court must notice it at any time (Rule 12(h)(3)).
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: 'From fact' vs. 'from law'. De facto segregation (as a matter of practice) doesn't violate Equal Protection without discriminatory intent; de jure (by law) does.
subject: General
note: Equal Protection intent rule from memory (Washington v. Davis).

hook: Bona fide = 'in good faith'. A BFP pays value and takes WITHOUT notice (actual, record or inquiry) of an earlier claim. The BFP is the star of every recording-act question.
subject: Real Property
note: Recording-act role from standard doctrine.

hook: 'Let the buyer beware.' The old default: the buyer takes the risk of defects. Modern law has shrunk it: UCC implied warranties (merchantability, fitness), implied warranty of habitability in new homes and leases, and seller disclosure duties.
subject: Contracts

hook: 'Beyond the powers': an act outside the authority of the corporation or public body. In Con Law, a federal agency acting without statutory authority is ultra vires.
subject: General

hook: 'Let the master answer': an employer is vicariously liable for torts an employee commits within the scope of employment (not independent contractors, and not a 'frolic'). Detour = minor deviation, still within scope; frolic = substantial departure, outside it.
subject: Torts
note: Detour/frolic from Restatement (Third) of Agency 7.07, from memory.

hook: 'As much as he deserved': reasonable value of services when no price was agreed, or no contract can be enforced. It is a restitution/quasi-contract remedy, not a contract price.
subject: Contracts

hook: 'A matter judged': claim preclusion. After a valid final judgment on the merits, the same parties (or privies) can't relitigate the same claim, including claims they COULD have brought. Issue preclusion (collateral estoppel) is the separate, issue-by-issue cousin.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: 'I do not wish to contend': a plea that doesn't admit guilt. Under FRE 410 a nolo plea (and withdrawn guilty pleas and plea-discussion statements) generally can't be used against the defendant later.
subject: Evidence
note: FRE 410 from memory; not fetched.

hook: 'By itself': inherently, without needing more proof. Negligence per se: violating a safety statute is itself the breach, if the plaintiff is in the protected class and the harm is of the type the statute targets.
subject: General

hook: 'Through the court': an opinion by the court as a whole, with no author named. Often short and used in emergency or summary cases.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: 'Friend of the court': a non-party who files a brief with information or arguments. Not a party; has no standing to appeal as of right.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: 'By the fact itself': automatically, by operation of the fact alone. Example: 'ipso facto' bankruptcy clauses are largely unenforceable in bankruptcy law.
subject: General
note: Bankruptcy example is our gloss; the Latin meaning is verified.

hook: 'With the necessary changes made.' Applies a rule to a new situation after adjusting the details. Useful in analogical reasoning on the exam.
subject: General

hook: 'While the lawsuit is pending': interim relief such as temporary alimony or a preliminary injunction while the case runs.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: 'A suit pending': a notice recorded against land warning buyers that litigation about the property is under way. It puts purchasers on notice, so they can't claim BFP status against the outcome.
subject: Real Property
note: Recording-act effect from standard doctrine.

hook: 'Parent of the nation': the state suing to protect the welfare of its citizens. A state can sue as parens patriae only for a quasi-sovereign interest, not merely on behalf of a few citizens' private claims.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Standing nuance from memory (Alfred L. Snapp & Son v. Puerto Rico).

topic: in rem / in personam / quasi in rem
hook: In personam = jurisdiction over the person (judgment against the defendant). In rem = against property to determine everyone's rights in it. Quasi in rem = a claim against the defendant's property in the forum unrelated to the dispute (Shaffer v. Heitner requires minimum contacts). Pennoyer v. Neff started the whole tangle.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Shaffer v. Heitner cited from memory (not in the fetched pages).

hook: 'From the beginning': void ab initio means never valid, as opposed to voidable (valid until avoided). Example: a contract with a minor is voidable at the minor's option, not void.
subject: General

hook: 'About the smallest things': too trivial for the law to care (de minimis non curat lex). A tiny deviation can still be a breach, but it is less likely to matter for damages or substantial performance.
subject: General

hook: 'Of the same kind': general words after a list are limited to things like those listed ('cars, trucks, and other vehicles' won't include aircraft). Canon of statutory interpretation.
subject: General

hook: 'It is known by its companions': an unclear word takes meaning from the words around it. Pair with ejusdem generis for statutory-interpretation questions.
subject: General

hook: 'Things done': old catch-all for the events of the case. The FRE broke it into specific rules (present sense impression, excited utterance, etc.), so the label rarely wins on the MBE.
subject: Evidence
note: Historical relationship from memory.

hook: 'Body of the crime' (not the corpse): proof that a crime occurred and someone caused it. Requires independent corroboration of a confession in many jurisdictions, so a confession alone isn't enough.
subject: Criminal Law
note: Corroboration rule from memory; jurisdiction-specific.

hook: 'Between the living': a transfer made during the donor's life (a deed or inter vivos trust), as opposed to by will. A gift inter vivos needs donative intent, delivery, and acceptance.
subject: Real Property
note: Gift elements from standard doctrine.

hook: Per stirpes = 'by the branch': each family line takes an equal share, and a dead beneficiary's share passes to her descendants. Per capita = 'by the head': equal shares to living takers. The Latin words are about WHO divides.
subject: Real Property

hook: 'Knowingly': awareness of wrongdoing or of a dangerous trait. Owner of a domestic animal is strictly liable only if he knew of its dangerous propensity (the 'one bite' idea), but is strictly liable for wild animals.
subject: Torts
note: Animal-liability rule from Restatement (Second) of Torts 506-509, from memory.

hook: 'Wrong in itself' vs. 'wrong because prohibited'. Murder is malum in se; an unlicensed-fishing violation is malum prohibitum. Strict-liability public-welfare offences tend to be mala prohibita.
subject: Criminal Law

hook: 'The reason for deciding' (binding) vs. 'a thing said in passing' (not binding). Only the holding, tied to the facts, binds later courts. A dissent is never precedent.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: 'For this turn': a lawyer licensed elsewhere is allowed to appear in ONE case. In My Cousin Vinny the whole joke is that the New York lawyer needs to be admitted in Alabama for this trial.
subject: General
note: Wikipedia film plot summary doesn't mention pro hac vice; the film's Alabama setting and the Judge's challenge to Vinny's credentials are consistent with it. Treat the film link as a mnemonic aid, not a legal source.

hook: 'In equal fault': a court won't help either of two equally guilty parties. Plaintiff who joined in an illegal bargain generally can't enforce it, with exceptions (e.g. withdrawal before performance, protected class).
subject: Contracts
note: Exceptions from Restatement (Second) of Contracts 197-199, from memory.

hook: 'To whose benefit?': ask who gains. Helps spot motive on Evidence 404(b) questions and in conspiracy hypotheticals.
subject: General

hook: 'Among other things': used when a list is only partial. Whenever you see it in a statute or holding, the list is illustrative.
subject: General

hook: 'Under the judge': the matter is before the court now. Common in the UK; in the US the phrase 'pending' does the same job.
subject: General

hook: Sub poena = 'under penalty'. A subpoena orders a person to appear; subpoena duces tecum ('bring with you') orders them to bring documents. Rule 45 governs subpoenas to non-parties in federal court.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Rule 45 from memory.

hook: 'Now for then': a court order corrects the record as if done earlier (clerical errors; see Rule 60(a)). It records what already happened rather than changing history.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Rule 60(a) from memory.

hook: 'Anew': the reviewing court decides the question without deference. Questions of law get de novo review on appeal; findings of fact are reviewed for clear error; discretionary rulings for abuse of discretion.
subject: General
note: Standards of review from memory.

hook: 'Of its own kind': unique. 'A sui generis category' means a new category that doesn't fit existing ones.
subject: General

hook: 'For the lawsuit': a guardian ad litem is appointed to represent a minor or incompetent person in this case only.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: 'From the stronger': if the weaker claim wins, the stronger one must. Handy for 'if a, then certainly b' arguments.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: 'Nobody's thing': ownerless property that the first taker may acquire. Wild animals, as Pierson v. Post shows, are res nullius until captured.
subject: Real Property

hook: 'Where there is a right, there is a remedy.' Underlies Marbury's claim that a legal right must have a legal remedy.
subject: General
note: Marbury quote about the 'right to a remedy' is from memory; Wikipedia page fetched covers only the Judicial review holding.

hook: 'Without which not': the but-for test for actual cause. If the harm would have happened anyway, the defendant wasn't a sine qua non cause. Substantial factor covers multiple sufficient causes.
subject: Torts
note: Latin phrase and test from standard sources; page not re-fetched.

hook: 'To one who is willing, no injury is done': the ancestor of assumption of the risk. Express assumption (a signed release) can bar a claim; implied assumption usually folds into comparative fault.
subject: Torts
note: Not in the fetched Wikipedia excerpt; standard doctrine.

hook: 'The expression of one is the exclusion of the other': if a statute lists X and Y, Z is probably excluded. Contrast ejusdem generis, which is about general words after a list.
subject: General
note: Not in the fetched Wikipedia excerpt; standard doctrine.

hook: Latin for 'elsewhere' (alius 'other' + ibi 'there'): the defense that you were somewhere else. A one-word Latin lesson you already speak.
subject: Evidence

hook: Verdict comes from Anglo-Norman verdit: veir 'true' + dit 'said'. It shares the truth-root with voir dire ('to speak the truth'). Hook for remembering both: the jury 'says the true thing'.
subject: General

hook: From Latin iurisdictio, 'saying the law' (ius 'law' + dicere/dictio 'say'). The power of a court to say what the law is. Subject-matter jurisdiction (the case type) and personal jurisdiction (over the defendant) are two separate hooks.
subject: General
note: Wiktionary confirms the Latin source word; the ius + dictio breakdown is standard etymology but was not on the fetched page.

hook: Tort is the Medieval Latin tortum, 'wrong, injustice', literally 'twisted', from the same root as torture and contort. A tort is a 'twisted' act: a civil wrong that isn't a breach of contract.
subject: Torts

hook: From Latin perjurare, per- + jurare 'to swear'. A false oath in court. The same iurare is behind jury: the jury is the group sworn to give a true verdict.
subject: Evidence

hook: From Medieval Latin iurata, from Latin iuro 'I swear'. Hook: Jury, perjury, juror, jurisdiction and just all feed from the Latin ius/iurare family.
subject: General

hook: A man running for a train drops a package of fireworks wrapped in newspaper; guards helping him board; it explodes; a coin scale topples on Helen Palsgraf far down the platform. Cardozo (4-3): negligence is a breach of a duty owed to THIS plaintiff, and 'the risk reasonably to be perceived defines the duty to be obeyed'. Andrews' dissent: duty to the world, limit by proximate cause. The foreseeable-plaintiff rule is the majority approach.
subject: Torts

hook: An 11-year-old lightly kicks a classmate's shin in a Wisconsin schoolroom; the boy's prior leg injury turns it into a disaster. The defendant is liable for the full harm: you take the plaintiff as you find him (the eggshell skull rule). For battery you need intent to make the contact; you don't need intent to cause that much harm.
subject: Torts

hook: A 5-year-old moves a lawn chair just as Ruth Garratt is about to sit. Intent for battery = purpose OR knowledge to a substantial certainty that the contact will result. No hostile motive needed. The court remanded for a finding on whether he knew.
subject: Torts

hook: Two hunters both negligently shoot toward a quail; one pellet hits their guide; no one can tell whose. The burden shifts to the defendants to prove they did NOT cause the harm (alternative liability); each is jointly and severally liable if they can't.
subject: Torts

hook: A barrel of flour falls from an upper window and hits a man on the street. No one saw how. The court (Baron Pollock) lets the accident itself serve as prima facie evidence of negligence: the birth of res ipsa loquitur.
subject: Torts

hook: A wooden wheel collapses on a 1910 Buick Runabout; the buyer sues Buick, not the dealer. Cardozo: no privity needed; a manufacturer owes a duty of care to foreseeable users of a product that is dangerous if negligently made. Privity dies in negligence cases.
subject: Torts
note: The maker of the wheel (Imperial Wheel Co.) is not named in the fetched source; omitted here.

topic: United States v. Carroll Towing (1947), the Hand formula
hook: Barge Anna C breaks free in New York Harbor with no bargee aboard. Learned Hand: liability turns on whether B < P x L: the Burden of precautions vs. the Probability times the gravity of the Loss. If the precaution is cheaper than the expected harm, skipping it is negligent.
subject: Torts

hook: A farmer rigs a spring-gun in an abandoned farmhouse to catch burglars; a trespasser loses most of his leg. Iowa Supreme Court: you may not use deadly force to protect property alone, whatever your 'No Trespassing' signs say. Compensatory $20,000 plus punitive $10,000.
subject: Torts

hook: A mill owner's reservoir bursts into abandoned mine shafts and floods the neighbor's colliery. English rule: bringing a dangerous thing on your land that escapes makes you liable ('non-natural use'). U.S. descendant: strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities (Restatement (Second) 519-520).
subject: Torts
note: Restatement sections cited from memory.

hook: A patient tells his therapist he intends to kill Tatiana; the therapist alerts campus police but not her. Held: when a therapist knows a patient poses a serious danger to an identifiable person, there's a duty to take reasonable steps to protect. 'The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins.'
subject: Torts

hook: A civil-rights ad has small errors about Montgomery police; the police commissioner wins $500,000. Unanimous reversal: a public official needs 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth) to win a defamation suit about official conduct. Later extended to public figures.
subject: Torts

hook: A delivery driver who swings a few blocks to buy lunch is on a DETOUR (employer still liable). One who drives 100 miles to see a friend is on a FROLIC (outside the scope of employment).
subject: Torts
note: Rule from Restatement (Third) of Agency 7.07, from memory; page not re-fetched.

hook: Made wrong (manufacturing defect: deviates from the intended design), Designed wrong (reasonable alternative design / risk-utility), Warned wrong (inadequate instructions or warnings). Strict liability for commercial sellers; negligence for the rest.
subject: Torts
note: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability 2; page not re-fetched.

hook: A mill's crankshaft breaks; the carrier delays delivery of the old shaft to the maker; the mill loses business. The carrier didn't know the mill was idle without it. Damages limited to losses that arise naturally from the breach or were reasonably in the parties' contemplation at contracting: lost profits denied.
subject: Contracts

topic: Lucy v. Zehmer (1954): the objective theory
hook: After drinks, Zehmer writes 'We hereby agree to sell to W. O. Lucy the Ferguson Farm complete for $50,000' and signs. He says he was joking. Held: enforced. A reasonable person would think he was serious, so secret intent doesn't matter. Myth buster: it was a restaurant receipt, not a napkin.
subject: Contracts

hook: An ad promises 100 pounds to anyone who catches influenza after using the smoke ball as directed, and says 1,000 pounds is deposited at a bank. Held: a binding unilateral offer to the world, accepted by performance, with consideration and clear intent (not puffery).
subject: Contracts

topic: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store (1957)
hook: An ad for a fur stole at $1 'first come, first served' IS an offer because it was clear, definite, and explicit and left nothing open. The first customer to arrive could accept. Ordinary ads are usually invitations to bargain; this one wasn't.
source: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, 251 Minn. 188, 86 N.W.2d 689 (1957)
subject: Contracts
note: Wikipedia URL returned 404; facts from memory of the reported case. Verify against the opinion.

hook: An uncle promises his nephew $5,000 if he stays away from drinking, smoking, swearing and gambling until 21. He does. Held: giving up a legal right is valid consideration, even if the promisee benefited. Detriment, not economic value to the promisor, is the test.
subject: Contracts

topic: Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864): the two ships called Peerless
hook: Cotton is to arrive 'ex Peerless' from Bombay; there are TWO ships Peerless, sailing in October and December. Each party meant a different ship. No meeting of the minds, so no contract. Classic mutual misunderstanding on a material term.
subject: Contracts

hook: A music hall rented for concerts burns down before the first date, through no one's fault. Performance became impossible; both parties are excused because the hall's existence was an implied condition. The roots of impossibility and impracticability.
subject: Contracts

hook: A builder uses Cohoes pipe instead of the specified Reading pipe in a country house; the pipes are of equal quality. Cardozo: substantial performance, and damages are the difference in value (almost nothing), not the cost of tearing out the walls. The 'wrong brand' case.
subject: Contracts

topic: Hawkins v. McGee (1929): the hairy hand
hook: A surgeon promises a '100 percent good hand'; a skin graft from the patient's chest leaves a hairy palm. Expectation damages: the difference between the promised (good) hand and the hand he got. Warranty by a doctor is enforceable as a contract.
subject: Contracts

hook: Acceptance by mail is effective when DISPATCHED (if properly addressed and the mail is a reasonable medium), but revocation, rejection and option acceptances are effective on RECEIPT. If the offeree sends rejection first and acceptance second, the one that arrives first usually controls in a close case.
subject: Contracts
note: Standard doctrine; Restatement (Second) 63; page not re-fetched.

hook: A buyer orders 'chicken' and gets stewing hens when he expected young broilers. Judge Friendly asks what the word means as used in the trade and by the parties and concludes the buyer hadn't proved his narrower meaning. Trade usage and course of dealing explain terms.
subject: Contracts
note: From memory; page not fetched this session.

hook: Post chases a fox with hounds on a beach; Pierson kills and carries it off. Ownership of a wild animal requires capture or mortal wounding, not mere pursuit. Livingston's dissent thought hunters' custom should decide. The first-possession case.
subject: Real Property

hook: A cattle feedlot and a growing retirement city (Sun City) collide. The feedlot is enjoined as a public nuisance, but the developer who 'came to the nuisance' must pay the feedlot's relocation costs. Equity can protect the public AND the earlier arriver.
subject: Real Property

hook: A buyer of a London square promises to keep the garden 'uncovered with buildings'; a later buyer with notice wants to build. Held: equity will enforce the restrictive covenant against a successor with notice. The origin of equitable servitudes: no privity required.
subject: Real Property

hook: A lawyer sues his absent client by publishing notice in a newspaper; he wins a default judgment, has Neff's Oregon land sold, and it is quickly assigned to Sylvester Pennoyer. Supreme Court: a state court can't bind a nonresident not served within the state; property must be attached first. Rule: territorial power.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: A Missouri-based shoe company with no Washington office but commissioned salesmen who showed samples in hotels. The State of Washington sues for unemployment-fund contributions. Held: jurisdiction exists if the defendant has 'minimum contacts' such that suit doesn't offend 'traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice'.
subject: Civil Procedure

topic: Burnham v. Superior Court (1990): 'Tag, you're it'
hook: A New Jersey dad flies to California for business and to see his kids; he is served with divorce papers there. Transient (tag) jurisdiction is constitutional even if the claim has nothing to do with the state. Scalia's plurality relied on tradition; Brennan on fairness.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: A bank sends only newspaper notice to known trust beneficiaries. The Court demands notice 'reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances' to apprise interested parties and give them a chance to object. Publication is fine for unknown people.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: The 'reasonably calculated' phrase is the standard formulation from the opinion; fetched summary used 'reasonably calculated'.

hook: Harry Tompkins walks along railroad tracks in Pennsylvania and a protruding object from a passing train costs him his arm. Brandeis: 'There is no federal general common law.' Federal courts in diversity apply state substantive law (and federal procedure).
subject: Civil Procedure

topic: Hertz v. Friend (2010): the nerve center
hook: For diversity, a corporation's 'principal place of business' is its nerve center: where the officers direct, control and coordinate the corporation's activities (usually headquarters), not where most business is done.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: A forgotten commission, a refused delivery, and a Supreme Court that says: you're right, but we can't help you, because Congress gave us more original jurisdiction than Article III allows. 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' Judicial review is born.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: An Ohio farmer grows extra wheat for his own farm and is fined under the quota law. Held: Congress may regulate activity that, in the aggregate, substantially affects interstate commerce. Home-grown wheat reduces demand for wheat on the market.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: A Klan leader's rally speech. Advocacy of force or lawbreaking is protected unless it is directed to inciting or producing IMMINENT lawless action and likely to do so. Intent + imminence + likelihood. Replaced 'clear and present danger'.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: A coach prays on the 50-yard line. The Court sides with him (6-3) and replaces Lemon/endorsement analysis with a test based on historical practices and understandings of the Establishment Clause.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: Overruled Roe and Casey: the Constitution doesn't confer a right to abortion; regulation gets rational basis review. Applies the Glucksberg test for unenumerated rights: 'deeply rooted in the Nation's history and tradition'.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: Clarence Gideon, charged with breaking into a Florida pool hall, asks for a lawyer, is refused, defends himself and loses. His handwritten petition wins 9-0: the Sixth Amendment right to appointed counsel applies to states in felony prosecutions. Retried with a lawyer, he was acquitted.
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: Ernesto Miranda confesses after two hours of questioning without warnings. Held 5-4: statements from custodial interrogation can't be used unless police first warn the suspect and obtain a valid waiver. Later limits: public-safety exception (Quarles), Dickerson (Miranda stays), Vega v. Tekoh (no section 1983 suit for a bare violation).
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: Police force their way into Dollree Mapp's Cleveland home looking for a bombing suspect, find obscene materials, and she is convicted. The Court (6-3) applies the exclusionary rule to the states: evidence from an unconstitutional search is inadmissible in state court.
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: An officer watches two men repeatedly peer into a store window and meet a third. He may stop them on reasonable suspicion based on specific, articulable facts, and pat down for weapons if he reasonably believes the person is armed and dangerous.
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: The FBI bugs a public phone booth. 'The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places.' Test (Harlan): actual subjective expectation of privacy that society recognizes as reasonable. Replaced the trespass test for most searches.
subject: Criminal Procedure

hook: A phone seized at arrest holds 'the privacies of life'. Held (9-0 in the judgment): police generally need a WARRANT to search the digital contents of a cell phone seized incident to arrest. The case is shorthand: phone = warrant.
subject: Criminal Procedure
note: Fetched Wikipedia page did not contain the 'get a warrant' quote; verify the quote against the opinion before using it.

hook: Four sailors adrift after the Mignonette sank; three kill and eat the cabin boy, Richard Parker, to survive. Held: necessity is not a defense to murder. Sentenced to death and then commuted to six months. Classic exam image for 'necessity cannot justify killing an innocent'.
subject: Criminal Law
note: English case, but it appears in American casebooks; the MBE tests the general rule (necessity generally not a defense to intentional killing).

hook: Gregory Lee Johnson burns a flag outside Dallas City Hall during the 1984 Republican convention. 5-4: flag burning is expressive conduct protected by the First Amendment (Spence test: intent to convey a message that observers will likely understand). Texas could not punish it.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: United States v. Lopez (1995): San Antonio, a gun, and the Commerce Clause
hook: A San Antonio high-schooler (Alfred Lopez Jr.) carries a concealed .38 into Edison High School. The federal Gun-Free School Zones Act is struck down (5-4): possessing a gun near a school is not economic activity and the statute had no jurisdictional link to commerce. The case that revived limits on the Commerce Clause.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: Sweatt v. Painter (1950): UT Law School
hook: Heman Sweatt is denied admission to the University of Texas School of Law because he is Black; Texas builds a tiny 'separate' law school in Houston. Unanimous: not equal (faculty, library, intangibles like reputation and alumni network). A stepping stone to Brown v. Board.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: San Antonio ISD v. Rodriguez (1973): rational basis for school funding
hook: Parents in the poor Edgewood district sue over Texas's property-tax school funding. 5-4: wealth is not a suspect class and education is not a fundamental right under the federal Constitution, so only rational basis applies. Classic 'low-level scrutiny' answer.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

hook: Pete Hernandez, a Mexican-American, is convicted by a jury drawn from a county that had excluded Mexican-Americans from jury service for decades. Unanimous: Equal Protection protects groups beyond the black/white divide when they are treated as a distinct class.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: Smith v. Allwright (1944): the white primary
hook: A Black dentist in Houston is denied a ballot in the Democratic primary. 8-1: because the state delegated election authority to the party, the party's whites-only rule was state action violating the Fifteenth Amendment. State action doctrine in one case.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

hook: Houston deputies find two men in a private apartment; Texas criminalized same-sex sodomy. 6-3: the law violates Due Process; Bowers v. Hardwick is overruled. Kennedy's opinion didn't use the 'strict scrutiny' label; Scalia's dissent called it 'an unheard-of form of rational basis review'.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

hook: Texas withholds funds for educating undocumented children and Tyler ISD charges them tuition. 5-4: the scheme violates Equal Protection. The scrutiny label is disputed (the Court did not call it strict scrutiny); remember the OUTCOME and that immigration status is not a suspect class.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law. Scrutiny level: sources characterize it differently; do not teach as a distinct 'level'.

hook: Texas sues in the Supreme Court (original jurisdiction) over bonds sold during the Civil War. The Court holds secession was never effective: 'an indestructible Union, composed of indestructible States'. Federalism and original jurisdiction rolled into one.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law. 'Indestructible Union' phrase is the case's well-known quote; fetched summary paraphrased it.

topic: Whole Woman's Health v. Jackson (2021): who can you sue?
hook: Texas SB 8 lets private citizens enforce the law through lawsuits. The Court allows a pre-enforcement challenge only against state LICENSING officials, not the state judges, clerks or the Attorney General: sovereign immunity and Ex parte Young limit the proper defendants. It did not decide whether the law was constitutional.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: Salinas v. Texas (2013): 'just stay silent' isn't enough
hook: In a voluntary, non-custodial interview a Houston man simply stops answering a question. The plurality: to claim the Fifth Amendment privilege you must expressly invoke it, and the prosecutor may then comment on the silence. 5-4, with no majority opinion.
subject: Criminal Procedure
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: Texas v. Cobb (2001): the Sixth Amendment is offense-specific
hook: Cobb has a lawyer on a burglary charge but confesses, after Miranda warnings, to the related murders of a woman and child. 5-4: the Sixth Amendment right attaches offense by offense (Blockburger test), so the confession on an uncharged offense is admissible.
subject: Criminal Procedure
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: Powell v. Texas (1968): status vs. act
hook: Leroy Powell, a chronic alcoholic, is convicted of public intoxication in Austin. 5-4: the Eighth Amendment doesn't bar punishing the public ACT of being drunk in public, unlike Robinson v. California (1962) which barred punishing the STATUS of addiction.
subject: Criminal Law
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law.

topic: Pennzoil v. Texaco (1985): the handshake that cost $10.53 billion
hook: Pennzoil thinks it has a deal to buy Getty Oil (handshake + memorandum of agreement). Texaco swoops in and buys Getty. A Houston jury awards $10.53 billion for tortious interference with contract (settled in 1987 for about $3 billion; sources differ on the exact figure). Formation hook: when is an agreement binding before the final papers are signed?
subject: Contracts
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law. The MBE's contract-formation rule is general (Restatement (Second) 27); the Pennzoil verdict details come from a web search summary, not the full opinions.

topic: Judge Roy Bean: the 'Law West of the Pecos'
hook: A saloon-keeper-turned-justice-of-the-peace held court in his Langtry, Texas saloon. Most of the famous stories (hanging judge, fining a corpse $40) are legend; the point for the exam is the opposite: courts have power only where law gives them jurisdiction (he couldn't grant divorces).
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Texas flavour only: the MBE tests the federal rule these cases created, never Texas-specific law. Wikipedia flags the famous anecdotes as reported, not verified.

topic: Texas hypo: the rancher's fence (adverse possession)
hook: A rancher moves a fence 40 feet onto a neighbor's pasture and runs cattle there openly, without permission, for the full statutory period. Elements: actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile, continuous (CHANGE). The period varies by state, so the exam will tell you.
source: ours (original mnemonic, checked against the cited rule text)
subject: Real Property
note: Illustrative hypothetical for the app; elements verified under CHANGE / Heluva sources.

topic: Texas hypo: the handshake cattle deal (UCC 2-201)
hook: A buyer and seller shake on 200 head of cattle at $1,200 each. Cattle are goods and the price is over $500, so a signed writing is needed unless an exception applies (payment accepted, goods received and accepted, admission, or a merchant's confirmation not objected to within 10 days).
subject: Contracts
note: Illustrative hypothetical for the app.

hook: A weekend rider signs a release before a bull-riding clinic and is hurt. Express assumption of risk via a clear release can bar a negligence claim; it generally can't excuse gross negligence or violations of public policy, and the release is read narrowly.
subject: Torts
note: Illustrative hypothetical; the enforceability of releases varies by state.

topic: Texas hypo: the oil under the fence line (rule of capture)
hook: Drilling on your land pulls oil from a pool that also lies under the neighbor's land. Under the traditional rule of capture the driller keeps what he produces; the neighbor's remedy is to drill his own well. Flavor only: oil-and-gas law is state-specific.
subject: Real Property
note: Not an MBE staple. Rule from memory; Wikipedia page not fetched. Use with caution.

topic: My Cousin Vinny: Mona Lisa Vito qualifies by experience
hook: The prosecutor challenges the girlfriend as an auto expert; she answers hard questions and is allowed to testify about tire marks. Real rule: an expert may be qualified by 'knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education' (FRE 702). The film predates Daubert (1993), and today the proponent must show it is more likely than not that the opinion is reliable.
subject: Evidence
note: ABA Journal confirms the 'experience' point and the pre-Daubert timing. Alabama state law governed the fictional trial, not FRE 702.

topic: My Cousin Vinny: cross-examining an eyewitness
hook: Vinny attacks perception and memory: obstructed sightlines, impaired vision, unreliable time estimates (the grits timeline). The techniques (perception, memory, bias) map to impeachment. Judge Posner called the film 'rich in practice tips'; Professor Bernabe says Vinny is 'terrible at the things we teach and very good at the things we don't'.
subject: Evidence

topic: My Cousin Vinny: ask for discovery
hook: Vinny tries a trick to see the prosecutor's file; Mona Lisa tells him he can simply demand it through formal discovery. In criminal cases the prosecution must also disclose material exculpatory evidence (Brady v. Maryland). A civil litigator's version of the same lesson: Rule 26 and Rule 34 requests.
subject: Civil Procedure
note: Plot point verified; the Brady link is our gloss, since the sources describe the discovery request only.

topic: My Cousin Vinny: attack the expert's basis
hook: The FBI examiner admits the tire is among the most common in the country, so the match proves little. That is Rule 702's 'sufficient facts or data' and 'reliable application' in action: an expert opinion is only as good as its foundation. Cross by getting the expert to concede the limits.
subject: Evidence

topic: My Cousin Vinny: the 'confession' is only an admission
hook: The sheriff reads the defendants' statement as a confession; they say they meant a minor theft. A party's own statement offered against him is not hearsay (FRE 801(d)(2)(A)); what it MEANS is for the jury. A Miranda issue would turn on custody and interrogation.
subject: Evidence
note: Minnlawyer article notes statements to police can be misinterpreted; the hearsay and Miranda links are our gloss.

topic: My Cousin Vinny: contempt and a skeptical judge
hook: Judge Haller repeatedly holds Vinny in contempt. Real law: a court may punish misconduct in its presence summarily (direct contempt), but needs notice and a hearing for contempt outside the courtroom (indirect). It's also a lesson in preserving objections with a straight face.
subject: General
note: Plot point verified (contempt); the direct/indirect contempt distinction is standard law from memory.

topic: Seinfeld finale: the 'Good Samaritan law' is really a duty-to-rescue law
hook: The four friends are prosecuted in Latham, Massachusetts, for failing to help a carjacking victim. In real law the general common-law rule is NO duty to rescue a stranger; Good Samaritan statutes protect people who DO help from lawsuits; a few states require reporting certain crimes. Exceptions: special relationship, you created the peril, you started a rescue and abandoned it.
subject: Torts
note: Source says Latham is a real Massachusetts town but had no duty-to-rescue law when the episode aired. The three duty exceptions are standard Restatement doctrine from memory.

hook: Juror 8 buys a switchblade like the murder weapon and shows the jury it is not unique. In a real trial, jurors may not bring outside facts into deliberation: after a verdict, a juror may testify only to extraneous prejudicial information, outside influence, or a clerical error (FRE 606(b)(2)). Whether the film's experiments cross that line depends on facts; courts differ.
subject: Evidence
note: The search found no authoritative analysis of the knife scene under 606(b); our link is analytical. Treat as a memory hook, not a rule application.

hook: The prosecution must prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt, and the jury must be unanimous in federal criminal trials (and, since Ramos v. Louisiana (2020), in state felony trials). The film's whole plot: one juror who won't accept a weak chain of inference.
subject: Evidence
note: Ramos holding from memory; page not fetched.

topic: Legally Blonde: impeach with an impossible alibi
hook: Elle exposes the witness by showing her story conflicts with a physical fact (a freshly permed head and a shower). That is impeachment by contradiction. Real life: courtroom confessions on cross are rare; commentators call the scene a 'Perry Mason moment' and note a first-year student wouldn't try a murder.
subject: Evidence

topic: Better Call Saul: Sandpiper Crossing is a class action (with RICO)
hook: Jimmy finds a pattern of overbilling at a nursing home and hopes to bring a class action. Real hooks: numerosity/commonality/typicality/adequacy (Rule 23(a)) and the RICO damages standing question (Sedima v. Imrex; Holmes v. SIPC), per a fan legal analysis.
subject: General
note: Search found no law-professor critique of Rule 23 details in the show. RICO is not tested on the MBE. Use only as a CANT(S) memory image.

topic: Cop shows: Miranda at every arrest
hook: On TV, officers read Miranda warnings at the handcuffs. In real law the warnings are required only before CUSTODIAL INTERROGATION when the state wants to use the answers; a suspect who volunteers statements, or who is arrested but never questioned, has no Miranda claim. Also: no warnings, no admission, but evidence can still come from other sources.
subject: Criminal Procedure
note: Generic TV trope, not tied to one show; the law side is verified.

topic: Monty Python's Dead Parrot: merchantability and revocation
hook: The Norwegian Blue is sold as a pet, but it is dead on arrival. In UCC terms the seller (a merchant) breached the implied warranty of merchantability (goods fit for ordinary purposes, UCC 2-314); the buyer can reject within a reasonable time or revoke acceptance if the defect was hidden and substantially impairs value, with notice (2-608). The shop-owner's offer of a replacement hints at cure (2-508).
subject: Contracts
note: UCC sections fetched. Applying them to the sketch is our playful gloss; the search found no law review analysis. A B.C. tribunal 'dead parrot' case used provincial sale-of-goods law, not the UCC.

topic: Home Alone: Kevin vs. the Wet Bandits (Katko v. Briney)
hook: Kevin booby-traps his house. Katko says you can't use deadly force to protect PROPERTY alone from trespassers. Complication: Kevin is a child at home facing burglars, so self-defense/defense-of-dwelling issues arise, and spring-gun cases involved empty buildings. The movie is a fun image of the rule, not a clean application.
subject: Torts
note: One legal commentary treats Kevin's blowtorch trap as like the spring gun; the search says the analysis is speculative.

topic: Wile E. Coyote v. Acme: a products-liability complaint
hook: Ian Frazier's 1990 New Yorker piece scripts the opening statement in a products-liability suit by a coyote against Acme. Good for remembering: manufacturer or seller defects (made wrong, designed wrong, warned wrong), foreseeable use, and the defendant's defenses (assumption of risk, misuse). A parody, not a real filing.
subject: Torts
note: Sources disagree on the exact publication date (Feb 18 or Feb 26, 1990); the legal theory in the piece is closer to warranty than to pure strict liability.

hook: Fine print signed by children, presented in a blur of fast talk. Two doctrines come to mind: unconscionability (procedural and substantive unfairness, judged at formation, UCC 2-302 by analogy) and capacity (a minor's contract is generally voidable at the minor's option).
subject: Contracts

topic: Suits: the lawyer who never passed the bar
hook: Mike Ross practices law with no license. Real law: practicing without a license is unauthorized practice of law, and lying about admission is a crime. Professional responsibility is the MPRE's job and isn't on the MBE or the NextGen foundational-concepts list.
subject: General

hook: Fix it (407 subsequent remedial measures), Settle it (408 compromise offers and talks), Pay the bills (409 offers to pay medical expenses), Plead it (410 withdrawn guilty and nolo pleas, plea talks), Insure it (411 liability insurance). None can prove fault or the validity of the claim, but each has an 'other purpose' door (407: ownership/control if disputed, feasibility if disputed, impeachment; 411: bias, agency, ownership, control).
subject: Evidence
note: Grouping is ours; the five rules were each fetched. Rule 408 has a limited criminal-case carve-out for negotiations with a government body in its regulatory/enforcement role; read the rule if the facts involve one.

hook: Relevant evidence may be excluded only if its probative value is SUBSTANTIALLY outweighed by unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, or needlessly cumulative evidence. Equal weight is not enough. Hook: 'substantially' is the thumb on the scale for the proponent.
subject: Evidence

hook: Three questions: (1) Is it an out-of-court statement? (2) Is it offered for the truth of what it asserts? (3) If yes to both: is it excluded by 801(d) (not hearsay by definition) or admitted by 803/804/807? Skip any step and you pick the wrong answer.
subject: Evidence

hook: Class of persons (plaintiff is within the group the statute protects), Harm type (the injury is the kind the statute was meant to prevent), Excuse (incapacity, emergency, compliance would be more dangerous). Violation of a safety statute is the breach if C and H are met and no E.

hook: Defamatory statement, Of and concerning the plaintiff, Published to a third party, Falsity plus fault (the First Amendment: public figures/officials need actual malice, per NYT v. Sullivan), Damages (presumed for defamation per se in many places). Opinion that can't be proven false isn't actionable.

topic: Strict in theory, fatal in fact
hook: Gerald Gunther's famous line for strict scrutiny: it is 'strict in theory and fatal in fact.' Not always: Korematsu (1944) upheld an exclusion order using a standard described as 'rigid scrutiny', and Grutter (2003) upheld a race-conscious admissions plan. But SFFA v. Harvard (2023) held the admissions programs failed strict scrutiny.
subject: Constitutional Law
note: Gunther quote and cases from memory; Wikipedia page not fetched. Verify before quoting.

topic: Rational basis: the challenger carries the burden
hook: Rational basis review: any conceivable legitimate government purpose, rationally related. The BURDEN is on the person attacking the law. Under strict and intermediate scrutiny the burden flips to the government. Rodriguez (Texas school funding) is the textbook example of rational basis.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: When Congress is silent and the state law discriminates against out-of-state commerce, it is almost per se invalid unless necessary for an important interest. When the law is neutral, it is invalid only if the burdens clearly exceed the local benefits (Pike balancing). Exceptions: market participant and congressional approval.
subject: Constitutional Law

hook: Substance goes to state law, procedure to federal. If a Federal Rule directly covers the point, follow the Rule (Hanna v. Plumer) as long as it is valid under the Rules Enabling Act and the Constitution; otherwise ask whether ignoring state law would encourage forum shopping or inequitable administration of the laws.
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: Claim preclusion (res judicata): same claim, same parties or their privies, valid final judgment on the merits, and it bars claims that could have been brought. Issue preclusion (collateral estoppel): the identical issue was ACTUALLY litigated and ESSENTIAL to a valid final judgment against the party. Defensive nonmutual use is allowed; offensive use is at the court's discretion (Parklane).
subject: Civil Procedure

hook: Rule 56(a): the court grants it when there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. The moving party starts with the burden to point to the absence of evidence (Celotex), and the court views the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-movant.

hook: A defendant can remove only a case that could have been filed in federal court originally, to the federal district embracing the state court. All served defendants must join, notice is due within 30 days of service, and in a diversity case a defendant who is a citizen of the forum state cannot remove (the forum-defendant rule).

hook: Imminent threat of unlawful force, Reasonable belief, Proportional response: deadly force only against a threat of deadly force or serious bodily harm. A majority of states impose no duty to retreat before using force (a minority require retreat if safe), and the aggressor generally loses the defense unless he withdraws.

hook: Probable cause (arrest, warrant, most searches): a fair probability. Reasonable suspicion (Terry stop and frisk): specific, articulable facts, less than probable cause but more than a hunch. The Terry frisk adds 'armed and presently dangerous'.
